text: Time to put this whole chapter together. Here's a real T-SQL table and query: customer_id as an IDENTITY one-one primary key, then a SELECT TOP 10 that uses ISNULL to display a fallback when phone is missing. Three pieces here don't translate literally into PostgreSQL: IDENTITY, TOP, and ISNULL.

First decision: IDENTITY one-one becomes GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY — the modern, standard-compliant PostgreSQL syntax. You'll also see the older SERIAL pseudo-type in existing code, which is really just an integer plus an auto-created sequence behind the scenes, but GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is the better choice going forward.
Second decision, the same move you made for MySQL back in Chapter Seven: TOP 10 moves from right after SELECT, to LIMIT 10 at the very end of the query, after ORDER BY.

Third decision: ISNULL simply doesn't exist in PostgreSQL at all. COALESCE replaces it directly — phone, comma, 'No phone on file' — and COALESCE works identically across every single dialect in this entire course.

Put all three together, and here's the fully translated PostgreSQL version — GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, LIMIT at the end, COALESCE in place of ISNULL. SELECT, FROM, ORDER BY, and the column list itself needed zero changes.

That's Chapter Eight, and the exact same lesson you learned translating to MySQL: most of a query is portable, and the real skill is spotting the handful of vendor-specific pieces. Next, Chapter Nine: Snowflake SQL, and what's genuinely different from T-SQL in the cloud warehouse world. See you there.
